828812fc4c:
This chapter is about deciding what goes into the context window on every call. It covers what that costs in tokens, seconds and dollars, and how to stop paying twice for the same tokens.

The chapter treats the window as a budget derived from a requirements card. Then it works through the levers in the order an architect should pull them:

  1. trim at the source;
  2. edit and compact what accumulates;
  3. isolate verbose work;
  4. cache the stable prefix, with the hit-rate arithmetic that decides whether caching pays;
  5. assemble prompts from versioned modules;
  6. load expertise on demand with Skills.

Governance is designed in: prompt versions, audit of what the model was told, retention of derived summaries, tenant isolation. The examples come from telecom care, network operations and retail, in Python and Java/Spring.
f003622886:
Reading time: 3.5 to 4 hours  ·  Companion code, 20 runnable examples for this chapter: ccarp-companion/05-context-caching-skills/ (run bash run_all.sh; every example works offline with --mock, and the caching examples run against a small simulator of the documented prefix-cache rules).

All prices, speeds, cache multipliers and hit rates in the examples are illustrative planning numbers. Before any figure goes into an ADR, check the docs for current prices, minimum cacheable lengths, parameter names and beta headers.

Where this chapter quotes a product detail, it says "at the time of writing". Those details change faster than the architecture does. Exam facts for CCAR-P come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint; verify them against the official exam guide.
70d7ecf87a:
The context window is a budget with three prices, money, seconds and attention, and you set it from the requirements card, not from the size of the window.

Spend that budget in a fixed order: stop tokens entering (trim at the source), stop them accumulating (edit, compact, isolate), stop paying full price for the ones that repeat (cache the stable prefix), and load expertise only when the task needs it (modular prompts, Skills), measuring after every step and keeping the audit trail that lets you say what the model was told.
df7e35c0b1:
Everything else in the chapter is that paragraph worked out with arithmetic.

The order matters because the levers are not equally safe or equally large.

  • Trimming a tool result before it enters the context has no side effects at all.
  • Clearing old tool results saves tokens, but it invalidates the cached prefix from the clearing point forward. Doing it every turn can cost more than leaving the results alone. The companion's example 03 measures exactly that, and the result surprises most people.
  • Compaction saves a great deal but loses detail, so it needs a facts block that is never summarised.
  • Caching saves the most per unit of risk. But only if the prefix is byte-identical and the traffic is dense enough for the entry to survive between requests. That is a hit-rate question, with a closed-form answer this chapter derives.

An architect who knows the sizes and the side effects can rank the levers for a measured system in a few minutes. An architect who knows only the names reaches for whichever one was in the last blog post.
c2c6d0d9cb:
The blueprint for Domain 2 asks you to reason about context windows and token usage, and to design for prompt reuse through caching, modular prompts and Skills.

Chapter 4 chose the model and shaped the prompt. This chapter decides what that prompt may carry on each call, how long it can grow, and how its repeated parts are paid for.

It also bridges into two other domains. Into Domain 4, because you find out whether any of this worked by measurement (ch 10 for observability, ch 11 and 12 for evaluation and optimisation). And into Domain 5, because every reuse mechanism creates an artefact: a cached prefix, a summary, a prompt version, a Skill. Each has an owner, a retention period and an audit question attached.

CCAR-F ch 14 covers case-facts blocks and context preservation as agent-design techniques. Here we take the architect's view of the same problem: token budgets, compaction trade-offs and the economics of the cache.
458ec78c19:
A Spring architect already has the right instincts for this chapter.

  • The window is a heap. The maximum is not the target; the working set is.
  • The prompt cache is a read-through cache in front of an expensive computation. It has a TTL, an eviction rule, a key (here, an exact byte prefix) and a hit rate that depends on access patterns more than on cache size.
  • Compaction is a log-compaction job. It keeps the latest state and discards the history, which is only safe if state and history are separate things.
  • A prompt registry is configuration management with an audit requirement.
  • Skills are lazy loading.

Keep those five analogies in your head and the mechanics below will feel familiar. The new parts are the token arithmetic, and the fact that the thing being cached, trimmed and compacted is the only information the model has.
1e3e0c532f: Every technique in this chapter is an old idea in a new place. Knowing the lineage tells you which old lessons carry over: nearly all of them. It also tells you which part is new. The thing being managed is the model's only source of information, so a mistake costs accuracy as well as money.
6a2cc75569:
The first version of the problem appeared when programs outgrew physical memory.

Peter Denning's working-set model (1968) gave the field its central observation. A program does not need all of its memory at once. It needs the pages it is currently using. A system that keeps the working set resident and evicts the rest runs near full speed. One that cannot hold the working set thrashes.

The same decade produced memoisation (Donald Michie, 1968): storing the result of a pure computation, keyed by its inputs.

By the 1980s every machine had a hierarchy of caches, and the discipline around them was settled. A cache is only as good as its hit rate. The hit rate depends on the access pattern more than on the size. And anything that makes the key unstable (a timestamp mixed into it) turns the cache into pure overhead.
589986416f:
Replace "page" with "token" and you have the context window. Think of the model's attention as acting on a working set that you assemble on every call.

Too small, and the answer lacks the fact it needs. Too large, and you pay for tokens that do not help. Worse, as section 03 explains, you dilute the ones that do. The window itself is merely the address space. What matters is what you keep resident.
d9a7730226:
The web turned the cache from a hardware detail into an architectural component with an explicit contract: Cache-Control headers, validators, TTLs. It also produced a long tail of production incidents caused by keys. Some varied when they should not (a session id in a URL). Others did not vary when they should (a user's page served to another user).

Content delivery networks made hit rate a line item that finance cared about. Telecom engineers know the same pattern from DNS TTLs and from provisioning caches in front of slow inventory systems.

Two lessons carry straight over to prompt caching. First, design the key before you design the cache: put what is shared in the key and what is personal outside it. Second, a cache that serves the wrong tenant's content is a security incident, not a performance bug. Isolation is part of the design (section 22).
fdb052cde9:
Transformers compute, for every token, a key and a value vector that later tokens attend to. During generation the model keeps these (the KV cache), so it does not recompute earlier tokens for each new one.

That state is a pure function of the token prefix. So two requests that start with identical tokens produce identical state for that prefix. Inference systems exploited this inside a single server first. Research systems such as vLLM's paged attention and SGLang's radix tree (both 2023) showed how to share prefix state across many requests efficiently.

The technique stayed an implementation detail until providers exposed it.
40d94ddae6:
Meanwhile the windows grew. GPT-3 (2020) took about 2,000 tokens. By 2023 vendors were shipping 100,000 and then 200,000 token windows, and some current models accept a million.

Bigger windows did not remove the problem. They moved it. Liu and colleagues' "Lost in the Middle" study (2023, published 2024) found that models used information at the beginning and end of a long input more reliably than information in the middle.

Practitioners now say context rot for the general effect: accuracy and recall degrade as the input grows. The Anthropic documentation says so directly. A larger window does not automatically mean better results, and curating what is in context matters as much as how much space is available (check the docs for the current wording).
9176f6c340:
Providers began exposing prefix reuse as a priced feature during 2024. You mark a breakpoint, and the provider stores the computed state for the prefix. A later request with the same prefix is billed at a fraction of the input price and starts generating sooner.

Anthropic's prompt caching is explicit about breakpoints, TTLs and multipliers. That is what lets you reason about it as an architect, rather than hope.

Agentic workloads then exposed the next problem. A loop that calls tools for fifty turns accumulates context faster than any window grows. The responses were a family of context-management features (check the docs for the current status of each):

  • clearing stale tool results and thinking blocks (context editing);
  • summarising on the server when input reaches a threshold (compaction);
  • a memory tool that lets the agent keep notes outside the window;
  • a framing for the whole subject that Anthropic's engineering team called context engineering.

Agent Skills (introduced in late 2025; check the release notes for the date) apply lazy loading to expertise itself. A few dozen tokens of metadata per Skill are always present, and the body loads only when the task matches.
9392a17114:
For the exam, the history matters for one reason: none of these features is magic. Each is a known systems idea with a known failure mode.

Can you say what a cache key is, why a timestamp breaks it, what log compaction loses, and why lazy loading needs a good index? Then you will answer scenario questions correctly, even when the scenario uses a feature name you have not seen.
bd365aaa0a:
Start with the property that makes everything else follow: the Messages API is stateless. Every request carries everything the model will see. In order, that is the tool definitions, the system prompt, every earlier turn (including every tool call and tool result), any documents and images, and the new message. The model's own output, including thinking tokens, has to fit in the same window.

No server-side conversation remembers anything between requests. The exception is a feature that stores something on your behalf, and then you should ask where and for how long.

The consequence is arithmetic. The cost of a turn is the cost of the entire conversation so far. The cost of a conversation of n turns is the sum of n growing requests.
5b202fc69d:
Two accounting facts matter for everything that follows.

First, total input is the sum of three usage fields. At the time of writing, the documentation defines input_tokens as only the tokens after the last cache breakpoint. So total input is cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens (check the docs). A dashboard that charts input_tokens alone shows a cache-heavy system as nearly free. That is the most common metering bug in production.

Second, thinking tokens count. They are billed as output, and they count against the window. On current models the previous turns' thinking blocks are kept by default, so they are billed again as input on every later request. (Older models stripped them automatically; check the docs for the model you use.) A long agent session with extended thinking therefore grows faster than the visible transcript suggests.
26c9dd6518:
Capacity today is large. At the time of writing, the documentation lists 1M tokens for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 and 200K for Haiku 4.5. There is no separate long-context surcharge on the 1M models, except for one model that prices prompts over 100K higher (check the docs; both facts have changed before).

If input alone exceeds the window, the API returns a 400 error ("prompt is too long"). That is the one hard failure. But a design that works until the window is full is a design that works until it fails. Three softer limits bind long before capacity does:
a94b908ba3: Latency. Time to first token grows with the number of input tokens the server must process. A prefix served from cache is processed much faster than a cold one; that is half the reason to cache. Fresh tokens still pay the full prefill cost. So the latency budget in your requirements card is also a token budget.
063b21b771: Attention quality. The relevant fact competes with every other token. Accuracy on retrieval-from-context tasks degrades as the input grows, and it degrades most for material in the middle. You cannot price this cost in dollars. It is the reason a cached 200K prompt can be cheaper and still worse than a curated 20K one.
eec01329d5:
So treat the window the way a JVM operator treats heap. The maximum is a safety bound. The target is a working set that fits with headroom. And a long-lived component that keeps accumulating garbage will eventually fail, in a way that is hard to diagnose after the fact.

The rest of the chapter is garbage collection (editing, compaction, isolation), allocation discipline (trimming, layout), and a very good L2 cache (the prompt cache).
90d8156ce5:
Do not carry a token count from one model to another. The documentation notes that Claude Opus 4.7 and later models use a newer tokenizer. It produces roughly 30 percent more tokens for the same text than earlier ones (check the docs). So a prompt budget tuned on one model is wrong on the next.

The token-counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens in the Python SDK) has these properties:

  • it accepts the same structure as a message request, including system prompts, tools, images and PDFs (images and PDFs as base64 only);
  • it is free to use, with its own requests-per-minute limit by usage tier;
  • it returns an estimate that can differ slightly from the billed count;
  • it does not support every server tool (check the docs for the list).

Use it in CI to enforce budgets, and in production for pre-flight checks on the largest requests. Use the usage object on the response as the source of truth for billing and dashboards.
4f724abfee:
A token budget assigns every component of the context a ceiling. You do not choose the ceilings. You compute them from three numbers on the requirements card of chapter 1:

  • a latency bound, typically a p95 time to first token for an interactive channel;
  • a cost ceiling per unit of work (per conversation turn, per case, per document);
  • a quality cap: the largest context size at which the per-segment evaluation still met its bar, found by running the eval at several context sizes.

The budget is the minimum of the three. The one that gives the minimum is the binding constraint.

Naming it matters, because it tells you which lever to pull. If latency binds, fresh tokens are the problem and caching helps. If cost binds, output tokens and fresh input are the problem. If quality binds, nothing in this chapter that merely reduces price will help. You need to reduce or restructure what the model reads.
dcb47a2b4b:
Take the care-agent example. The card says:

  • p95 time to first token under 2.5 seconds on the chat channel;
  • at most $0.03 per customer turn;
  • the evaluation showed per-segment accuracy falling below the bar once the total context passed 40,000 tokens.

Companion example 01 derives the ceiling for each, with illustrative speeds and prices. Assume a measured p95/p50 ratio of 1.5, so the p50 target is 1.67 seconds. Assume a fixed 0.5 second before prefill starts, a prefill rate of 15,000 uncached tokens per second, and ten times that for cached tokens. With a 12,000-token cached prefix and 350 output tokens at a mid-tier price, the three limits on fresh (uncached) input per turn are:
a3e29d0b21:
Read the table the way the exam wants you to read it.

  • Design A sends everything fresh, 28,000 tokens. It exceeds the cost bound by more than a factor of three, even though it would have passed the latency bound.
  • Design B caches a 12,000-token prefix and keeps 6,500 fresh tokens per turn. It fits every bound, with the cost bound binding at about 7,000.
  • Design C caches the same prefix but lets 19,000 fresh tokens in (a generous retrieval top-k and unclipped tool results). It passes the latency bound and the quality bound, and fails the cost bound.
  • Design D trims further, to 4,000 fresh tokens.

The point of the exercise is the "binding" column. In all four designs it is cost, not latency. That tells the team that engineering effort on first-token speed would have been wasted.

The next thing to do is shave fresh tokens. The easiest ones to shave are in the tool results and the retrieved passages, not in the system prompt that is already cached.
e6d48ae7f2:
The last step is to split the binding limit across the components that make up the fresh input. That gives the budget table the agent's code then enforces.

For design B, the cost bound of about 7,000 fresh tokens becomes roughly 2,500 for history, 1,750 for tool results, 1,750 for retrieved passages and 1,050 for case facts and the question.

The split is a judgement. The shares come from measuring which component the evaluation is most sensitive to. What is not a judgement is that the pieces sum to the limit. A budget whose parts add up to more than the bound is a wish.
1b7450b625:
Two refinements before leaving the card.

First, budgets differ per segment. A premium-tier chat channel may have a looser cost ceiling and a tighter latency bound than a back-office batch process. So the same agent can run with different budgets under different routes. Per-segment requirements are literal.

Second, the quality cap is an empirical number, and it is model-specific. It moves when you change model, tokenizer or prompt. So it belongs in the evaluation harness (ch 11) as a regression test. Run the eval at 20K, 40K and 80K of context, padded with irrelevant but realistic material, and record where it falls over.
6f263c6350:
The measure-before-change rule of this guide has a specific meaning for context. You cannot rank levers until you know three things for your own traffic:

  • how many tokens each component contributes;
  • how many of the input tokens were served from cache;
  • how those numbers move over the length of a session.

The API gives you the second directly and the first indirectly.
dcb738a581:
The usage object on every response reports input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens. At the time of writing, it also reports a cache_creation breakdown by TTL (check the docs). The identity from section 03 lets you reconstruct total input.

The per-component split takes more work. Count each component in isolation with the token-counting endpoint (system alone, tools alone, the message list alone), and subtract the baseline of a trivial request. The sums are approximate because there is some framing overhead. But the proportions are reliable enough to rank levers.

Do this once per release in CI. In production, sample one request in a hundred for the full attribution.
6746de947d:
The numbers above are a toy, but they show the shape.

The first call writes 7,368 tokens to the cache, so it costs about six and a half times a later call. The next three read the same 7,368 tokens at the cache rate and cost $0.0046 each. And a dashboard that plots input_tokens shows 209 for every call, understating real input by 29,472 tokens across four calls.

If your capacity planning, or your showback to business units, reads that field, it is wrong. And it is wrong in the direction that causes a budget surprise.
6ca04da651:
What to put on the dashboard is a short list. Each item answers a question that a lever depends on.

  • Fresh input tokens per request by feature, with p50 and p95: is the working set growing?
  • Cache hit rate by tokens, by feature and prompt version: did the last release break the prefix?
  • Tokens by component, sampled: which term is largest?
  • Cost per resolved conversation (not per call): is the unit economics still the one on the card?
  • Peak-to-median context size per session: is a long tail of sessions responsible for most of the bill?

The fifth is usually the surprise. Context size per session is heavy-tailed, so the mean misleads. The p95 session often accounts for a third or more of the spend. That is the population that editing and compaction exist for.
e3dcd99c02:
One governance note belongs here, because metering is where it starts. Log token counts, component sizes, prompt keys and hashes. Do not log prompt contents, unless your retention policy for prompt contents has been set deliberately.

The metrics above are enough to run the system. The contents are a regulated data set (customer proprietary network information, payment data). Write them only to the audit store, with its own retention and access rules (section 22).
e83a04e3f5:
Quadratic growth is why a session that felt fine at turn 10 is expensive at turn 40 and broken at turn 80. It is also why the quantity to watch is peak context per session, not mean tokens per request.

And it is why every lever in this part of the chapter acts on the history term. Caching changes its price: history becomes cache reads, about a tenth of the base rate at the multipliers used in the examples. But caching does not change its size. Editing and compaction change its size. Isolation keeps it from being created.

The companion's example 03 simulates the same 40-turn session under six strategies, and checks the closed form against the simulation.
574643595d:
Three results in that table deserve a slow read.

Caching alone cuts the cost of the session by 82 percent without touching the context size. The peak context is still 113,000 tokens. That is cheap to pay for, but still a long way into the region where attention quality degrades.

Clearing old tool results every turn shrinks the peak to 37,000 tokens and the cumulative input to 1.05 million. And yet it costs more than caching alone ($1.65 against $1.35). Every clear edits the middle of the prefix and forces the system to rewrite the cache from that point on. Thirty-seven cache rewrites at the write premium outweigh the saved reads.

Clearing in batches, only when the context passes a trigger, makes seven edits instead of thirty-seven. That brings the cost down to $1.17, with a peak of 40,000 tokens.

The lesson is not "clear less". It is that the unit of design is the cache edit, not the token. An edit has a cost, and the policy should minimise the number of edits per token removed.
7f44477f90:
A note on thinking blocks, because they change the curve for reasoning-heavy agents. On current models the API keeps prior assistant thinking blocks in the context by default (older models stripped them automatically). A model producing 1,500 thinking tokens a turn adds that much to every later request as input.

The context-editing feature includes a strategy for clearing thinking blocks, with its own cache consequences. Keeping them preserves the cache. Clearing them invalidates it from the clear point (section 09; check the docs for the per-model default).

If your agent uses extended thinking and your session curves are steeper than the transcript length suggests, look here first.
a522262d53:
Position changes outcomes. Long-context models use information at the start and the end of the input more reliably than information in the middle. This is a property of how attention behaves over long sequences, not a bug in one product.

The practical rules follow from it, and from the cache.

  • Put what must never be missed near the start of the messages, in a labelled block: the case facts, the constraints the customer stated, the key findings of earlier work.
  • Put long reference documents before the question that uses them, not after it. Restate the question as the last thing in the final user message.
  • When you concatenate many sources, lead with a short index or summary. Wrap each source in tags with an identifier, so the model can locate and cite them.

Do not rely on a fact being "somewhere" in 200,000 tokens of transcript.
29a66c956a:
Layout also has a cache dimension that the attention rule does not: anything volatile must come after anything stable.

A case-facts block is stable within a case but changes between cases. So it sits after the shared prefix and before the turn history. The current question is volatile, so it is last.

The resulting order, from the first byte to the last, is: tools, system prompt (role, guardrails, policy), case facts, earlier-conversation summary, retrieved documents, question. It happens to be the order that both attention and caching prefer, which is a reason to trust it.
15dac7c593:
Layout is a policy, so enforce it in code, not by convention.

Companion example 04 assembles the messages from case facts, a ranked document list clipped to a token budget, a summary and the question. A checker fails when the facts are not at the start, the question is not last, or a required fact is missing. The checker runs in unit tests with no model. That is how you catch the regression where a refactor moved the question to the top.
61e5ea04c9:
CCAR-F chapter 14 teaches the case-facts block as an agent-design technique: what goes in it, why it is never summarised, how it survives a handoff. From the architect's chair the questions are different.

  • How many tokens may it occupy? A few hundred. If it is growing past a thousand, the case model needs restructuring.
  • Who owns its schema? It is an interface between the agent and the systems that read the case afterwards, so it is versioned like one.
  • What happens to it in the audit trail? It is the compact record of what the agent believed at each turn. That makes it the most useful single artefact for a reviewer.
a3084bf2ba:
The first lever is also the safest, so it comes first.

A tool that returns forty fields when the task needs four puts thirty-six fields into the context. There they are carried by every later turn, billed on every later request, and read by the model as if they mattered.

Trimming the result before it enters the message list has no cache side effects, because nothing earlier changes. It needs no summarisation call. It cannot lose information the task needed, if you chose the fields properly. And it reduces both the cost and the attention noise.

In practice it is the largest single saving in most tool-using agents. And it happens in the tool wrapper, which is code you own.
232fcb3be4:
The design rule is an allowlist per task, not a blocklist per tool.

A billing lookup serves several tasks. Explaining a bill needs the invoice lines and the last payment. A port-out check needs only the plan and the account status. A retention offer needs tenure and plan. Each task names the fields it may see. An unknown task fails closed, with an error that tells the model what is allowed, rather than returning the whole record.

This is a token control and a data-minimisation control at once. If no task needs the date of birth or the last four digits of an identifier, the model never receives them. So they cannot appear in a response, a summary, a cached prefix or a log.
f0336bf287:
Run the numbers the way the budget does. A raw record of 586 tokens, carried for the remaining 12 turns of a session, is 7,000 tokens of input. The projected 26-token result is 312. That is a 96 percent reduction on that term. The example output shows the cost as dollars per thousand calls.

Three other trimming techniques follow the same logic.

  • Return identifiers, not blobs. A search tool returns ten hits with id, title and a 200-character snippet. A separate get_document tool fetches the one the model chooses.
  • Paginate with a default limit. A log query returns the first 20 lines and a cursor, and the description tells the model how to ask for more.
  • Summarise at the tool boundary when the summary is deterministic. A tool that reads a week of cell alarms should return counts by severity and the three worst events, computed in code. It should not return 4,000 lines for the model to count.

The tool description is part of the cached prefix and part of the budget, so tighten it too. See chapter 6 for the tool-catalogue side of the same problem: too many tools is trimming's mirror image.
ee11e8482b:
Tool results are the fastest-growing part of an agent's context, and the least durable. Most are needed for the step that requested them and for a few steps afterwards.

Context editing removes old tool results (and optionally the tool call inputs) once the context passes a threshold. It leaves a placeholder so the model knows something was cleared. It can do the same for old thinking blocks.

At the time of writing it is a beta feature of the Messages API. You pass a beta header and a context_management object with a list of edits. Each edit type has its own trigger and retention settings. The names are versioned and the feature is changing. So treat the code below as the shape, and check the docs for current names, defaults and supported models.

You can also do the same thing yourself, client side, because you own the message list.
07a6847d27:
Read the parameters as a cost model, because that is what they are.

  • trigger sets when clearing begins.
  • keep sets how many recent tool interactions survive.
  • clear_at_least is the guard that matters most. The documentation states that clearing invalidates the cached prompt prefix from the point of the first cleared block. It recommends this parameter so that each clear removes enough tokens to justify the invalidation. That sentence is section 06's second lesson in one line.
  • exclude_tools protects results that the agent needs for the entire session. It is the same instinct as the pinned facts block: if a result will be needed again, do not clear it, or persist its content somewhere the agent can find it.
0bf8ce1376:
Define the terms first:

  • D is the number of tokens from the first block you would clear to the end of the context;
  • X is the number of tokens the clear removes;
  • R is the number of turns still to come;
  • r is the cache read multiplier and w the cache write multiplier (both relative to the base input price).

Without the clear, the next request reads all D tokens from cache at r. With it, the D − X remaining tokens must be written afresh at w. Every later turn then saves X·r relative to carrying them.

So the clear costs an extra (D − X)·w − D·r once, and saves X·r per turn. It breaks even after [(D − X)·w − D·r] / (X·r) turns. Solving for the smallest worthwhile clear gives Xmin = D·(w − r) / (R·r + w). That is the value to feed to clear_at_least, if you can estimate R.

The dollar saving understates the benefit, because a smaller context is also faster and more accurate. The formula is the conservative test.
4436bccd51:
The table says two things. Clearing 40,000 of a 60,000-token tail with ten turns to go breaks even after 4.8 turns, so do it. Clearing 8,000 of the same tail breaks even after 73.8 turns, so do not, unless the session is expected to run eighty more turns.

The check against the simulated cache agrees in direction. Over twelve turns, with a 30,000-token region cleared halfway, the cleared session cost $0.32 against $0.37 for the uncleared one.

Section 22 revisits this as an anti-pattern. A policy of "clear old results on every turn" is the same as setting X to one turn's worth of tokens, which the formula rejects.
1a5fdc6190:
Two operational cautions.

First, clearing removes information from the model's view. So persist anything important before it is cleared, into the facts block or an external memory the agent can read back. The placeholder tells the model a result existed, not what it said.

Second, the message list is no longer the transcript. Once results are cleared, the context cannot answer an auditor who asks what the agent saw at turn 12. Write every tool result to your own audit store at the time it is received, keyed by session and turn. Treat the context as a working copy.
b2be1bc166:
Compaction replaces the older part of a conversation with a summary when the context crosses a threshold. The session then continues from the summary plus recent turns. It is how very long sessions survive. Claude Code compacts automatically, and on /compact.

The Messages API offers server-side compaction as a beta context-management strategy. You enable a compaction edit with a token trigger. When input reaches the trigger, the API produces a summary block, and subsequent requests start from that block and what followed.

At the time of writing (check the docs):

  • the strategy is named compact_20260112, behind the beta header compact-2026-01-12;
  • the trigger is expressed in input tokens, with a documented default and a documented minimum (150,000 and 50,000 as fetched);
  • a custom summarisation instruction replaces the default prompt rather than extending it;
  • a flag can pause the response after the summary, so you can re-insert recent turns.

The compaction pass is billed too, and usage is reported per iteration. A dashboard that reads only the top-level usage fields will miss the summarisation tokens (check the docs for how to total them).
3888483a7f:
A summary optimises for gist. It keeps the story: what the customer wanted, what was tried. It drops specifics: amounts, dates, identifiers, promises made, constraints the customer stated, the exact wording of a condition. Those are the facts that make a care or billing conversation correct. They are also the facts a summariser is least likely to keep.

The architectural answer is to separate transactional facts from narrative.

  • Facts go into a structured block with a schema. A forced tool call extracts them so the values are verbatim. They are verified against the transcript and never summarised.
  • Narrative goes through the compactor, with an instruction not to restate the facts.

After compaction the context is: pinned facts, then the narrative summary, then the recent turns.

CCAR-F chapter 14 gives the mechanics of the block. The architect's addition is the audit. After every compaction, a test asserts that every required fact is still present in the new context.
f7b922bf96:
The scripted run is deliberately blunt. The naive summary ("Customer reported two outages and asked for compensation; agent opened a request") loses all six required facts. Those include a promised callback time, and a constraint that the customer must not be moved off a promotional plan. With the pinned block, the audit finds nothing missing.

The third line shows the other half of the design: the verbatim check. The extractor invented a fact ($180.40, when the transcript says $18.40). It is rejected before it can be pinned, because every extracted value must appear in the transcript it came from. Without that check, you have built a mechanism for making hallucinations permanent.
7e2a99e54a:
When to compact is a trade between two costs.

Compact too early, and you pay for many summarisation calls and many cache rewrites (compaction rewrites the whole suffix of the prefix). You also get many chances to lose a detail. Compact too late, and every turn carries a huge context.

Example 08 puts the pieces on one curve for an 80-turn session:

  • the token cost of the turns;
  • the summariser calls on the small model;
  • the cache rewrites after each compaction;
  • the expected cost of lost detail (an assumed 2 percent chance per compaction that a needed detail is dropped, at an assumed $40 per miss).
7e8302e835:
The shape is the point. At a 20,000-token trigger, the session compacts 76 times and the expected loss swamps everything. At 300,000 it never compacts and pays the largest token bill. The minimum sits in the interior.

And the minimum moves earlier when facts are pinned. With the summariser no longer responsible for the details, the expected loss per compaction falls by an order of magnitude. Compacting at 90,000 then beats compacting at 150,000.

That is a design argument for the pinned block, in numbers. It does not just protect quality. It makes a cheaper compaction policy affordable.

The inputs here are assumptions. Yours come from the compaction audit pass rate and the cost of an error on the card.
406e12d84e:
Some work is verbose by nature: searching a codebase, reading twenty runbooks, scanning a week of alarms for a cell cluster. If the lead agent does it, those tokens enter its context and stay until you compact or clear them.

A subagent does the reading in a fresh context and returns a condensed result. The lead sees a 1,500-token answer where it would have seen 90,000 tokens of source. This is the bounded context of domain-driven design, applied to attention. The detail stays inside the boundary, and only the contract crosses it.

Chapter 3 covers when to decompose and how to orchestrate. The budgeting question is narrower. What does the boundary save? What does it cost? And what keeps it honest?
382b9deb7e:
With the arithmetic in the example, the lead's context is 24,500 tokens instead of 210,000. Ten more lead turns cost $1.00 instead of $6.36, even after paying for three subagent runs on the small model.

The savings are real. The failure mode is equally concrete: the boundary is only as good as its contract. A subagent told to "investigate the alarms" returns too much, or the wrong thing, or a confident summary the lead has no way to check.

The contract should state the question, the maximum length, the required structure (findings with a source reference for each, and a confidence note), and what to leave out. Validate it in code before the lead sees it. Reject returns that are over budget, or that carry a finding without a reference.
30e1b43fa0:
Isolation has three costs. There are the subagents' own tokens, which are often cheap, because the subagent can run on a smaller model at low effort. There is orchestration latency. And there is summary fidelity.

Fidelity is the one to evaluate. Build a test set of questions whose answers are in the 190,000 tokens. Ask the lead directly and via subagents, and compare accuracy per segment. If the subagent path loses accuracy on a segment, the contract needs a field for whatever the summary dropped.

Where the exploration is retrieval over a known corpus, a retrieval pipeline (ch 8 and 9) usually beats a reading subagent on both cost and latency. The exam answer that prefers it is correct more often than candidates expect.
6c4c5ac6ee:
Processing a prompt means computing, for every input token, the internal key and value state that attention reads. For a prefix that is identical across requests, that work is repeated for nothing.

Prompt caching stores the computed state for a prefix. It reuses it when a later request begins with exactly the same tokens. A hit is billed at a fraction of the base input price and lets the server skip the prefill for those tokens, so time to first token falls as well.

A miss that writes a new entry is billed at a premium over the base price. So the feature is a bet: you pay more now for the chance of paying much less later. Whether the bet wins depends on the hit rate, which depends on traffic. Section 13 derives that dependence.

This section is about the rules that decide whether a hit is possible at all.
72e6fde3b5: The hierarchy. A change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it. Edit a tool definition, and the tools, the system prompt and the messages are all invalidated. Edit the system prompt, and the tools survive (if they were breakpointed) while the system prompt and messages are invalidated. Edit a message, and only the messages from that point onward are invalidated.
256b7efdde: Breakpoints. You mark a content block with cache_control, with at most four breakpoints per request. A single top-level cache_control field turns on automatic caching. That places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block and moves it forward as the conversation grows (it uses one of the four slots). Marking a block writes exactly one cache entry, at that block.
0ff744d5ea: Lookback. From a breakpoint, the system checks at most 20 positions backward for an existing entry. The documentation counts the breakpoint itself as the first position. It counts a run of consecutive tool-use blocks, or of consecutive tool-result blocks, as one. A conversation that grows by more than about 20 blocks between requests, with a single breakpoint at the end, misses. The fix is a second breakpoint partway through.
5b6eccbc60: TTL. Five minutes by default, refreshed at no extra charge each time the entry is read. An optional one-hour TTL costs a higher write price. The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that wrote or read the entry.
423a1a7cdd: Minimum length. A prefix shorter than the model's minimum is not cached, and no error is returned. The minimum is model-specific and has varied from 512 to 4,096 tokens across models (for example, 512 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 and 4,096 on Haiku 4.5 as fetched; check the docs). Reading the usage fields is the only way to know.
867dffab77: Settings that invalidate. Changing tool_choice, or adding or removing images anywhere in the request, invalidates the cached messages (but not the tools or system). Toggling certain server tools or features such as citations affects the system and messages. Changing thinking parameters or the effort setting invalidates the messages and, on some models, the system and tools too. Treat any per-request setting that is not constant as a cache hazard, and check the invalidation table for your model.
f2fb6cb420:
You can learn these rules by reading the page or by watching them. Companion example 10 implements them in a small simulator (cache_sim.py). It wires the simulator into the fake client so the usage fields come back populated, and asserts eight of the rules.

The simulator is a teaching model of the documented behaviour, not Anthropic's implementation. Its value is that you can now test your own request builder against the rules without an API key. Section 24 uses it that way.
64977b164c:
Read the tuples.

  • Rule 2 causes most production incidents. A single timestamp at the top of the system prompt turns each of three requests into a 3,002-token write with zero reads. That is the worst of both worlds: you pay the write premium each time and never collect the discount.
  • Rule 3 shows the TTL being refreshed by use. Three gaps of 200 seconds all hit, because each read resets the clock. Then the entry expires after 301 seconds of silence.
  • Rule 5 is the silent one. With a minimum of 4,096 tokens, a 3,000-token prefix returns no error and no cache. A team that migrates to a model with a different minimum loses caching without a single failing request.
  • Rule 6 shows the hierarchy, and rule 7 the lookback. A conversation that jumped 24 blocks past its earlier breakpoint wrote everything again. One with an extra breakpoint partway read 287 tokens back from the earlier entry.
d5b2153bf2:
The pricing structure is simple. At the time of writing, a five-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the base input price, a one-hour write costs 2 times, and a read costs 0.1 times on most models. The documentation lists lower read multipliers for some models, for example 0.05 for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 as fetched. Check the docs, and note that every example in this chapter takes the multipliers as parameters.

So a prefix read once for every write breaks even almost immediately: two requests at 1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35 against 2.0 uncached.

The tempting conclusion is that caching is always worth turning on. It is not. The number of reads per write is not a constant of your design. It is a property of your traffic, and you can compute it.
d803b79a91:
Three design consequences fall out of the curve.

  • Hit rate is per prefix, not per system. A system with 6 requests a minute in total is a 99 percent hit-rate system if they share one prefix. It is a poor one if they are spread over fifty prefixes (section 15).
  • The knee is steep. Between 0.05 and 1 request per minute per prefix, the five-minute hit rate goes from 22 percent to 99 percent. So the same code is a bad deal at night and a good one at noon. Look at the traffic by hour, not only the daily mean.
  • The 1-hour TTL is not an upgrade. It raises the write price from 1.25 to 2. It wins only when avoiding rewrites after gaps between 5 and 60 minutes repays the premium.
ead14d60eb:
Real traffic is rarely Poisson, and for it the decision is cleaner in terms of gaps. Let q1 be the share of gaps between 5 and 60 minutes, and q2 the share above 60 minutes.

  • A gap under five minutes is a hit with either TTL.
  • A gap between 5 and 60 minutes is a miss at 1.25 with the short TTL, and a hit at 0.1 with the long one.
  • A gap over an hour is a miss at either: 1.25 against 2.0.

The long TTL is cheaper exactly when q1·(w5 − r) > q2·(w1h − w5). At the default multipliers that is q1/q2 > 0.65. In words: use the one-hour TTL when moderate gaps are at least two thirds as common as long gaps.

Example 11 checks the rule against five arrival traces run through the simulated cache.
dad1505ddd:
Trace C is the one to remember. An internal tool used once every fifteen to twenty-five minutes looks like a perfect caching candidate: a big stable prefix, a repeating pattern. At the five-minute TTL it loses money, because every request is a miss at 1.25. The same tool is a clear win at the one-hour TTL (0.17 of the uncached price).

Trace E is the opposite. Three-hour gaps between twenty-minute bursts mean the one-hour premium buys nothing.

Nothing in the code differs; the access pattern does. A scenario question expects this kind of reasoning when it describes the traffic in a sentence and asks which TTL to use.
3b81ccb575:
A final refinement for cost-sensitive systems. The multipliers differ by model, so the thresholds do too. At a read multiplier of 0.05, the break-even condition becomes e−λT < 0.95/1.2 = 0.79, a very slightly lower floor on traffic. The structure of the argument does not change, and neither does the importance of measuring the gap distribution.

Do the sum with the multipliers from the pricing page on the day you write the ADR, and write the date next to them.
7fece721c2: Stable before volatile, always. Anything that changes per request, per user or per minute goes after the last breakpoint, in the final user message. That includes timestamps, request ids, user names, account ids, A/B arm labels, feature flags and retrieved passages.
1cd140c39f: Deterministic serialisation. If any part of the prefix is generated from data, generate it the same way every time: tools sorted by name, JSON keys sorted, no random ids, no locale-dependent formatting. The prefix is hashed as bytes, so whitespace counts.
d9d3d61aa4: Breakpoints at stability boundaries. Put one at the end of the tools block, one at the end of the system prompt, and one at the tail of the conversation (or use automatic caching for the tail). Keep a spare slot. A breakpoint belongs at the boundary between content that changes quarterly and content that changes daily, so a daily change does not invalidate the quarterly content.
58ffc07baf: Constant request settings. Do not vary tool_choice, image presence, thinking configuration or effort within a conversation without checking the invalidation table. If two routes need different settings, make them different conversations, with different prefixes, on purpose.
12acb20e49: Here is the commonest broken request, with all three problems in it, and the fixed version. The broken one has the current time and the customer's name at the top of the system prompt. It embeds JSON in the prefix with unsorted keys. And its tools are in an arbitrary order.
3d84da3d69:
The Java version is worth a second look, because it is a real trap for this reader.

A HashSet or HashMap-backed registry iterates in an order set by hash codes and capacity. Adding one tool reshuffles the order. A different JVM version may reorder it again. The tools block is the very first part of the prefix, so that reshuffle invalidates every cached entry for every route.

The symptom is a hit-rate cliff at each deployment that recovers over five minutes. It looks exactly like a cold start, so it gets ignored. A TreeMap or an explicit sort fixes it permanently.
e05c10f37f:
Companion example 13 turns the checklist into a linter. On the broken request, it reports the volatile text, the unsorted tools, the unsorted JSON and the per-user text near the start. On the fixed one, it is silent.

It then proves the point with the simulated cache, sending five requests a minute apart with a changing timestamp. The broken builder gets 0 cache reads in 5 requests. The fixed one gets 4 (the first request is the write).
9001b28444:
A request with a stable system prompt, a stable tool set and a growing conversation wants three breakpoints.

  • The first, on the last tool definition, caches the tools alone. A change to the system prompt then still reads the tools.
  • The second, on the last system block, caches tools plus system. That is the shared prefix across every conversation.
  • The third, at the tail of the conversation, caches the history so far. With automatic caching the API moves it forward each turn. With manual placement you move it yourself.

The fourth slot is the spare. Use it for a mid-conversation breakpoint when the history can grow by more than 20 blocks between requests (long tool loops). That is the lookback rule from section 12.

Do not use all four by reflex. Each breakpoint is an entry written at the write price. A breakpoint in a place that will never be read separately from its neighbour is pure cost. Place one where the content after it changes more often than the content before it.
60b0a1a25f:
Hit rate is computed per prefix, so splitting the prefix divides λ.

The usual cause is well-intentioned personalisation. A system prompt begins with the tenant's brand voice, the market's regulatory language, or the segment's offers, followed by the shared policy. Now take twelve tenants, one prefix each. The shared 9,000 tokens that were identical across all of them are now cached twelve times. Each copy sees a twelfth of the traffic, and the small tenants see almost none.

The fix is ordering. Shared content goes first, with its own breakpoint. The segment block goes second, with its own breakpoint. Personal data goes last. The shared prefix is then written once and read by every tenant, and each (small) segment block is written once per segment.
90d6f677c2:
The output shows the effect with identical traffic and identical content. Reordering the same blocks takes the token hit rate from 90 to 98 percent, and the cost from $9.23 to $6.21 per thousand requests. That is a 33 percent saving that required no new feature.

The tenant-first design looks respectable at 90 percent, because the two busiest tenants carry most of the traffic. The damage is in the tail tenants. Their traffic, and therefore their cost, is where the unit economics of a multi-tenant product are won or lost. Look at hit rate per prefix, not only in aggregate.
84ebd2f1ca:
An entry can be read only once the request that writes it has begun to respond (check the docs for the exact availability rule). Suppose a batch job or a traffic spike starts forty requests together against a cold prefix. None of them finds an entry, and all forty pay the write premium for the same 12,000 tokens. The cost is real, and invisible in unit tests.

The remedy is one warm-up request, awaited until it starts responding, followed by the fan-out. The same applies after a deployment that changes the prompt, after a TTL lapse over a quiet period, and when a new tenant's first burst arrives.

Example 19 simulates forty requests inside half a second, with a 1.5-second availability delay.
8aa4b36b33:
A new prompt version is a new prefix, so the first requests after a rollout are misses. A canary deployment at 10 percent of traffic splits the traffic across two prefixes. For the duration, it halves (or worse) the hit rate of both.

None of this is a reason not to roll out. It is a reason to:

  • schedule rollouts for periods of high traffic, where the cache rewarms in seconds;
  • warm the new version before shifting traffic;
  • include the cache-write cost of each rollout in the ADR's run-cost estimate;
  • put the hit rate on the rollout dashboard, so a change that unexpectedly breaks the prefix shows up as a cliff that does not recover.

Section 18 covers the registry mechanics that make the rollout controlled.
d504e0976b:
Caching has a narrow effect. Architects who know its limits avoid several recurrent mistakes.

It reduces the price of input tokens and, for long prefixes, the time to first token. Here is what it does not do.

  • It does not reduce output cost. For long answers or heavy thinking, output is often the larger term. In the contract-assistant scenario of section 26, output is 9 percent of today's bill, 17 percent after the cache fix and 36 percent after the other fixes. So the next lever is effort and answer length, not another cache.
  • It does not reduce window usage. Cached tokens still count toward the window and still compete for attention. Caching a 200,000-token prompt makes it cheap, and leaves it just as likely to bury the relevant fact.
  • It does not improve or degrade accuracy by itself. Cached processing should be equivalent to uncached, but the evaluation is how you know for your workload. So verify that a caching change did not alter behaviour.
  • It does not change the decode speed. A latency problem dominated by output length is untouched.
f308affda8:
There is one subtle interaction with latency. A cache hit shortens time to first token. That matters most when the prefix is long and the answer short. For a long answer streamed at a fixed token rate, decoding dominates total time, and the saving is a small fraction of the total.

If the requirement is a p95 for the complete answer rather than the first token, the budget in section 04 must include output tokens divided by decode speed. Then the cheapest latency lever is a shorter answer. Quote the latency requirement exactly as the card states it before choosing a lever.
97de4d0555:
As an organisation builds more Claude features, prompts duplicate. The same personal-data rule appears in twelve system prompts, each slightly different. The brand-tone paragraph has been edited in three of them and not the other nine. A fix to the credit-approval wording takes a week, because nobody can find every copy.

Shared libraries solve this problem in code, and the same solution applies. Factor the prompt into modules (guardrails, role, policy, output format, route-specific instructions). Version each module. Assemble every route's prompt from a manifest that lists which modules, at which versions, in which order.

You get one place to fix a rule and consistent behaviour across features. Each route's prompt is smaller and cleaner, because it includes only what it needs. And each module is a unit that can be evaluated and reviewed on its own.
556e59f711:
The ordering of modules is not a stylistic choice. Module order is cache order, and the ordering rule falls out of section 12. Put first the modules shared by the most routes and changed least often.

Organisation-wide guardrails go first, then the role, then the domain policy, then the format, then the route-specific instructions. A change to a route-specific module then invalidates only that route's suffix. A change to the guardrails invalidates everything, which is as it should be for a rule that applies everywhere.

Example 14 sorts the modules by (number of routes using it, descending; change rate, ascending) and gets exactly this order.
395d43466b:
The blast-radius lines are the output to put in a pull request.

  • A change to guardrails/org forces every route to rewrite its whole prefix (8,702, 5,002 and 5,602 tokens).
  • A change to policy/outage_credits costs one route 3,402 tokens and leaves the others untouched.
  • A change to route/dispute costs one route 802 tokens.

Before a module change ships, the author sees how many tokens of cache it will invalidate. The author also sees which evaluation suites it has to re-run: those of the routes that include the module.

That second part is the real value of modularity for governance. A module is the unit of review, the unit of evaluation and the unit of rollback. And the manifest is the record of what each route was told.
d737d27435:
Modularity has a cost, and the exam's "simplest architecture that works" rule applies. With two routes and one author, a registry of nine modules is overhead.

It starts to pay in two cases. One is when the same rule is maintained in three or more places. The other is when a regulated rule (disclosure wording, retention, a credit limit) must be provably identical everywhere.

Below that threshold, a file per route in version control, reviewed like code, is enough. Above it, the manifest and the checks in the next section are cheap insurance.
9466b690e4:
A prompt registry is configuration management for prompts. Each assembled prompt has:

  • a name and an immutable version;
  • a record of its modules and their versions;
  • the evaluation results it shipped with, per segment;
  • an owner;
  • a content hash.

Applications request billing-answer@v14, not a file path. Four properties make it a control rather than a folder.
